summary: RADIUS was running short of room in its 8-bit Attribute Type space, and experience showed a need for grouping attributes and carrying more than 253 octets of data. This document defines changes to RADIUS to solve these problems.

plainLanguage.summary: RADIUS packs information into attributes, and each attribute used to have a number from 1 to 255. RFC 6929 gives the protocol a second number per attribute, a way to group attributes inside one another, and a way to send an attribute larger than a single packet.

subtitle: Extends RADIUS with more attribute types, nested groups, and a way to carry data larger than one attribute.

tldr.problem: RADIUS has one 8-bit number per attribute type, and the RFC expected that space to run out by 2014 or 2015. The old grouping method had proved impractical, several attributes needed to carry more than 253 octets of data, and some vendors were close to using up their own vendor-specific space.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6929 borrows one octet from the attribute value to add an Extended Type number, adds a Long Extended Type that can carry fragments of a large value, and adds TLV, Extended-Vendor-Specific and integer64 data types.
tldr.outcome: The type space becomes a tree, the standard space gains roughly 1500 extended values, and vendors gain more than 1500 vendor-specific values. Older servers and proxies still read the new attributes because the Length field keeps its old meaning.

facts.label: Maximum text length with Extended Type

today: RFC 6929 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. It updates RFC 2865, RFC 3575 and RFC 6158, and it has not been obsoleted or updated since.

sections.title: Why RADIUS Needed Extending
sections.content:
RADIUS is the protocol a server uses to check who is connecting to a network. Its messages carry attributes, and each attribute starts with a type number. Under current allocation pressure, the RFC expects the RADIUS attribute type space to be exhausted by 2014 or 2015, so new specifications needed somewhere else to go.

Three further problems had shown up in practice. The attribute grouping method defined in RFC 2868 had proved impractical and needed a more powerful mechanism. Several attributes had been defined to transport more than the 253 octets of data originally envisioned, and each one was handled as a special case inside implementations instead of as a general method. Some vendors were also close to allocating all of the attributes in their own vendor-specific space.

RFC 6929 answers with two new attribute formats, three new data types and a new naming scheme. The author notes that the changes are the result of compromises, balancing flexibility, room in the RADIUS message, compatibility with existing deployments and difficulty of implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: RADIUS identifies each piece of information with a number, and only 256 numbers are available. This RFC adds a second number to each attribute, lets attributes hold groups of other attributes, and lets one attribute be spread over several pieces of a message.

sections.title: The Extended Type Format
sections.content:
The Extended Type format borrows one octet from the value of an attribute and uses it as a second type number. The Type field is identical to the Type field of the attribute format defined in Section 5 of RFC 2865. The Length field is one octet and covers the Type, Length, Extended-Type and Value fields together; permitted values are between 4 and 255. An Extended Type attribute received with a Length of 2 or 3 MUST be treated as an invalid attribute.

The Extended-Type field is one octet, and no values are allocated for experimental or implementation-specific use. Values 241 to 255 are reserved and MUST NOT be used. The Extended-Type is meaningful only within the context defined by the Type field, so the pair can be thought of as a new type space written as Type.Extended-Type. A RADIUS server or client MAY ignore attributes with an unknown pair, and implementations supporting this specification MUST use the pair to decide how to read the Value field.

Adding the octet lowers the maximum length of attributes of type text or string from 253 octets to 252. An attribute that needs to carry more than 252 octets MUST use the Long Extended Type format.
sections.plainLanguage: The new format keeps the old type number and length field and adds one extra byte that holds a second number. Together the two numbers say what the value means. A reader that meets an unknown pair is allowed to ignore the attribute.

sections.title: Carrying Values Larger Than One Attribute
sections.content:
The Long Extended Type format inserts one more octet between the Extended-Type octet and the Value field. Its Length field is one octet, with permitted values between 5 and 255; a Length of 2, 3 or 4 makes the attribute invalid. The extra octet is split into a one-bit More flag and seven reserved bits that implementations MUST set to zero when encoding and SHOULD ignore on reception.

The More flag says whether the current attribute holds more than 251 octets of data. It MUST be clear if the Length field is less than 255, and it MAY be set when Length is 255. When More is set, the attribute MUST have a Length of 255, another attribute MUST follow, and that next attribute MUST have the same Type and Extended-Type. Fragments of one value MUST be in order and MUST be consecutive attributes in the packet, and the last attribute in a packet MUST NOT have More set. RADIUS does not support fragmentation across packets.

Interpretation happens only after the fragments are reassembled, and the length of the data is the sum of the fragment lengths. If the reassembled data does not match the expected format, all the fragments MUST be treated as invalid attributes and the data discarded. The maximum size of a fragmented attribute is limited only by the RADIUS packet length limitation of 4096 octets, not counting headers and overhead, and implementations MUST be able to handle a fragmented attribute that completely fills the packet.
sections.plainLanguage: A value too big for one attribute is split into pieces that sit next to each other in the same message. A one-bit flag marks the pieces that have more to come. The pieces are joined back together before anyone tries to read the value.

sections.title: Grouping Attributes with TLV
sections.content:
The tlv data type is an encapsulation layer that lets the value of an attribute contain new sub-attributes, which can in turn contain values of data type TLV. The format reuses the RADIUS attribute format: a one-octet TLV-Type, a one-octet TLV-Length and one or more octets of TLV-Value. The TLV-Length covers all three fields and MUST have a value between 3 and 255. Values 254 and 255 of TLV-Type are reserved, and the value 26 has no special meaning and MUST NOT be treated as a Vendor-Specific Attribute.

The TLV-Value field is limited to 253 or fewer octets of data. The TLV-Value field SHOULD encapsulate a standard RADIUS data type, and it MUST NOT contain data using the Extended Type formats.

TLVs may contain other TLVs. When they do, the container TLV MUST be completely filled by the contained TLVs, so its TLV-Length MUST be exactly two more than the sum of the contained TLV-Length fields. A container that is overfilled is invalid. The depth of nesting is limited only by the TLV-Length field, which results in a limit of 126 levels, but nesting depths of more than 4 are NOT RECOMMENDED: they have not been shown to be necessary and they appear to make implementations more complex. Where an implementation does not support deep nesting, the unsupported layers are recommended to be treated as invalid attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: A TLV is a box inside an attribute value that holds more attributes. Boxes can go inside boxes. The RFC keeps the inner data small and asks that boxes rarely be nested more than four deep, because deep nesting makes programs harder to write and can look like an attack.

sections.title: Vendor Data and Bigger Counters
sections.content:
The evs data type, for Extended-Vendor-Specific, lets an attribute value carry a Vendor-Id, then an EVS-Type, then vendor-defined data. The four octets of the Vendor-Id are the Network Management Private Enterprise Code of the vendor in network byte order, and the EVS-Type is one octet whose values are assigned at the sole discretion of the vendor. The evs type MAY be used in attributes of Extended Type or Long Extended Type format and MUST NOT be used in any other attribute definition. It has no Vendor-Length field: the length of the EVS-Value is the length of the encapsulating attribute minus the attribute header, the Extended Type octet, the Vendor-Id and the EVS-Type, which is eight less than the Length field for Extended Type attributes and nine less for Long Extended Type attributes.

The integer64 data type carries a 64-bit unsigned integer in network byte order, so counters can pass 2^32. The expected use is in Accounting-Request packets, but it SHOULD be used in any packet where 32-bit integers are insufficient. Attributes with data type integer64 MUST have the Length field set to eight more than the length of the attribute header: ten for standard space attributes and TLVs, eleven for Extended Type attributes and twelve for Long Extended Type attributes.

The RFC also widens the Vendor-Id field of Vendor-Specific Attributes to the entire 4 octets of the Vendor field. RFC 2865 had defined it as 3 octets with the fourth set to zero. There is no immediate impact, because the largest Private Enterprise Code still fits in 16 bits, but support for four octets is RECOMMENDED.
sections.plainLanguage: Three smaller additions ride along with the new formats. One lets a vendor put its own numbered attributes inside an extended attribute. Another holds a 64-bit counter, so byte counts can pass the old 32-bit ceiling. The last widens the vendor number to four octets.

sections.title: Naming and Numbering Attributes
sections.content:
RADIUS attributes have traditionally been identified by a unique name and a number, for example the attribute User-Name has the number 1. The RFC extends this with a dotted number notation similar to the one used for Object Identifiers, written as Type.Extended-Type. An attribute in the type space of 241 with an Extended-Type of 1 is identified as 241.1. A TLV adds another level, so 241.1.1 identifies the TLV with type 1 inside attribute 241.1, and the sequence 245.2.3.4 identifies attribute 245, Extended-Type 2, of type TLV, containing TLV type 3, containing TLV type 4.

Vendor-Specific Attributes, which have the attribute number 26, can be identified in the same way as 26.Vendor-Id.Vendor-Type. The RFC notes that there are few restrictions on the size of the numbers at each level, and implementations SHOULD be capable of handling 32-bit numbers at each level.

The naming rules are recommendations: specifications SHOULD give attributes names that are globally unique across all RADIUS attributes, and a vendor SHOULD use its own name as a prefix for its attribute names. TLVs SHOULD be named with a unique prefix shared among related attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: Attributes now get a path of numbers instead of a single number, like 245.1.1 for an attribute inside a group inside another attribute. The same scheme gives vendor attributes a unique number that a name alone could not.

sections.title: Living With Older RADIUS
sections.content:
Some vendors had used attribute type codes from the reserved space in their own dictionaries. The RFC calls this antisocial behaviour and recommends that client and server implementations delete all references to those improperly defined attributes. Failing that, servers should have a per-client flag choosing between interpreting them as non-standard vendor attributes and interpreting them as Extended Attributes, with the default being the Extended Attributes format.

The RFC also defines the term invalid attribute. It means that the Length field lets the packet be accepted as not malformed, but the Value does not follow the format required for that attribute's data type. A packet holding an invalid attribute MUST NOT be discarded and MUST NOT be treated as a negative acknowledgment; only the invalid attribute is treated specially. An implementation SHOULD silently discard it, and MUST NOT handle it as if it were well formed. The property SHOULD NOT be treated as transitive, so an attribute that contains one bad TLV is not itself invalid, unless a TLV definition requires particular sub-TLVs to be present with particular values.

Proxy servers need special care, because they must forward attributes they do not understand. Proxy servers SHOULD forward attributes, even attributes they do not understand or that are not in a local dictionary, and SHOULD send them verbatim with no modifications. That includes invalid attributes, since another system in the network may understand them. The only exception is when local site policy requires filtering. Testing performed in 2010 via the EDUROAM service found that many proxies did not follow this practice: some filtered out unknown attributes, some truncated them to the expected length, some discarded the request entirely, and the rest passed them verbatim. The RFC therefore recommends that all proxies that do not support attributes 241 through 246 define them as being of data type string and delete all other local definitions for those attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: The new attributes stay readable to software that predates this RFC, because the length field still means the same thing. Proxies are told to pass attributes along unchanged even when they do not understand them, since something else on the path may.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document defines new formats for data carried inside RADIUS but otherwise makes no changes to the security of the RADIUS protocol. Attacks on cryptographic hashes are well known and improve with time. The security of the RADIUS protocol depends on MD5, which has security issues, and it is not known if those issues apply to RADIUS. For other issues, the RFC incorporates by reference the security considerations of Section 5 of RFC 6158.

As with any protocol change, code changes are needed to implement the new features, and those code changes can introduce new vulnerabilities. Since the RADIUS server performs network authentication, it is an inviting target for attackers, so access to RADIUS servers SHOULD be kept to a minimum.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC does not change how RADIUS is protected. It notes that RADIUS relies on MD5, that the server is a tempting target, and that the code changes needed for the new formats can bring their own bugs.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Same meaning as the Type field of the RFC 2865 attribute format.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the whole attribute; permitted values are 4 to 255.

fields.name: Extended-Type
fields.desc: Second type number, meaningful only within the context of the Type field. Values 241 to 255 are reserved.

fields.name: Value
fields.desc: One or more octets whose format is a valid RADIUS data type.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Same meaning as the Type field of the RFC 2865 attribute format.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of this fragment; permitted values are 5 to 255.

fields.name: Extended-Type
fields.desc: Second type number, as in the Extended Type format.

fields.name: M (More)
fields.desc: Set when this fragment carries more than 251 octets of data and another fragment follows.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero by senders, ignored by receivers.

fields.name: TLV-Type
fields.desc: Type of the sub-attribute; values 254 and 255 are reserved.

fields.name: TLV-Length
fields.desc: Length of this TLV including its header; MUST be between 3 and 255.

fields.name: TLV-Value
fields.desc: One or more octets, at most 253 octets of data, that may hold further TLVs.
